design_detail: Review article (JAMA, 'Review' section) comparing crack cocaine (the smoked base form) with cocaine hydrochloride (snorted or injected) on prevalence, chemistry, pharmacokinetics and effects, liability to repeated use, patterns of use, progression to dependence, and medical, psychiatric, social and criminal consequences, written to inform the debate on the US federal 100:1 crack-to-powder sentencing ratio. The structured abstract and Methods describe a MEDLINE search (1976–1996, four terms, names of selected authors), reference lists, manual searches of selected publications and an annotated bibliography, with inclusion limited to studies comparing crack with intravenous or intranasal hydrochloride. But no counts of records or included studies, no list or table of included studies, no appraisal and no quantitative synthesis are reported; the authors say almost all studies found were included; and many cited sources (survey and emergency-department reports, sentencing and crime reports, treatment and cost studies, an unpublished observation by one author) lie outside the stated criterion. 85 references, no tables or figures. Classified as a narrative review and appraised with the editors' checklist rather than AMSTAR 2 for these reasons. Differences between crack and powder are described, never tested.
can_establish: How the comparative evidence on crack and cocaine hydrochloride looked in 1996 to two laboratory and clinical researchers, and their argument that route, speed and size of effect, and amount and frequency of use explain most differences between the two forms, with pointers to the primary laboratory, survey, treatment and administrative studies.
cannot_establish: The size or certainty of any difference between crack and powder (no appraisal, no pooling, selection not reproducible); that snorting powder leads to crack use (a 'gateway'), which sequence data cannot show; that crack-associated harms are caused by the form or route rather than by amount, other drug use, social context or selection; anything about route-specific physical harms (respiratory, cardiovascular, injection-related), which the review does not cover; or present-day patterns (the evidence dates mostly from the mid-1980s to early 1990s).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Sources named: MEDLINE 1976–1996 searched with 'smoked cocaine', 'crack cocaine', 'freebase' and 'cocaine-base' and with names of selected authors; reference lists of original and review articles; manual searches of selected publications; an annotated bibliography on cocaine (p. 1581, Methods › Data Sources). The authors state that most studies were conducted in the mid to late 1980s and early 1990s (p. 1581, Data Extraction).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Methods: to be included a study had to compare crack with cocaine hydrochloride given intravenously or intranasally (p. 1581). The abstract states a broader criterion (comparison of routes or of types of cocaine) and an English-language restriction that the Methods do not mention (p. 1580). The authors say almost all studies found were included because so few existed (p. 1581).
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors' own; the yield of the search and the included studies are not reported. Most evidence on dependence and consequences comes from treatment-seeking, hotline, jail and street samples, and the review notes these surveys date mostly from the mid to late 1980s and may not reflect later patterns (p. 1583). The human laboratory comparison of smoked and intravenous cocaine comes largely from the second author's laboratory.

exposure.measurement: Varies across cited studies: laboratory administration with venous or arterial plasma assays; self-reported form and route in surveys and treatment samples; emergency-department and medical-examiner mentions in the Drug Abuse Warning Network (DAWN).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Forms and routes compared: cocaine hydrochloride snorted or injected; cocaine base (crack or freebase) smoked; oral use mentioned for timing only. Laboratory conditions cited include a choice study at doses giving similar plasma levels (50 mg smoked vs 32 mg intravenous; p. 1583) and absorption of intranasal doses in one study (58% of a 96-mg dose vs 30% of a 64-mg dose; p. 1582). Survey studies classify people by usual or initial route and by frequency.
exposure.polysubstance: The review notes that people using either form use other licit and illicit drugs heavily, people using crack more so, and names polydrug use and use of several routes by the same people as limits on interpretation (pp. 1584, 1586). Adjustment in a cited comparison is mentioned only for the neonatal-cost study (prenatal care, maternal alcohol and cigarette use, race, gravidity, maternal age, infant sex; p. 1585).

comparison.controls: Within-review comparisons of smoked crack with snorted or injected cocaine hydrochloride, and of people using crack with people using other forms of cocaine or other drugs.
comparison.matching: Not applicable. The review states that when the amount of cocaine used is controlled, no differences remain across routes, citing three sources (refs 39, 53, 54; p. 1584).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not addressed for most comparisons; the review notes that people selling crack were involved in deviant behaviour before crack, suggesting recruitment of people already involved in crime (p. 1585).

outcomes.instruments: Cited measures: venous and arterial plasma cocaine concentrations; cardiovascular and subjective effects; laboratory self-administration choices; survey items on route, frequency and transitions between routes; time from first to regular use; treatment entry; DAWN emergency-room and medical-examiner mentions; psychiatric diagnoses (Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia and Research Diagnostic Criteria), suicide attempts and psychiatric hospitalizations; sexual behaviour, HIV and other sexually transmitted infections; neonatal hospital costs and length of stay; arrests, weapons and criminal history.
outcomes.operationalization: Liability to repeated use (the authors' 'abuse liability') is framed as depending on the immediacy and magnitude of effect; dependence is described through faster progression to regular use, problems and treatment entry rather than through diagnostic criteria; consequences are compared by route or form without adjustment in most cited studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, without pooling (primary studies not read): no difference in elimination half-life between smoked base and intravenous hydrochloride in several studies, and 56 vs 78 minutes for smoked vs intranasal in one small study; urinary excretion of cocaine and metabolites 64%–69% of the dose for all three routes in one study; bioavailability of smoked base 60–70%, of intranasal cocaine from 25% to 80–94% across studies; peak venous concentration about 30–40 minutes after intranasal and about 5 minutes after intravenous or smoked use; peak arterial concentration about 10 times venous, within 15 seconds against 3–6 minutes for venous, after both smoked and intravenous use (one meeting abstract) (p. 1582). In one choice study, experienced participants chose smoked over intravenous doses giving similar plasma levels, although 80% preferred intravenous use outside the laboratory (pp. 1582–1583). 75–90% of people who smoked crack had first used cocaine intranasally; in one VA sample 52% of those starting intranasally switched to smoking; two thirds of people smoking crack used daily against 18% of people snorting powder; in the 1991 NHSDA, crack use was 52.5% among frequent and 17.5% among infrequent past-year cocaine use, and injection 24.3% vs 9.3% (pp. 1581, 1583). 1992 DAWN emergency-room mentions: smoking 37%, injection 18%, snorting 11%, other 4%, unknown 30% (p. 1584). Suicide attempts 2 to 4 times as common with crack as primary drug as with other primary drugs among people entering therapeutic communities (p. 1584). Neonatal costs $6735 vs $1226 and stays 7.9 vs 2.9 days when mothers reported crack rather than other cocaine, adjusted (p. 1585). Federal crack vs hydrochloride offenders: weapons 27.9% vs 15.1%; highest criminal-history category 17.6% vs 7.0% (p. 1585).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. The statement that differences disappear when amount is controlled rests on three sources (refs 39, 53, 54), two of them proceedings of the 1982 and 1983 meetings of the Committee on Problems of Drug Dependence, before crack appeared by the review's own account (mid-1980s; pp. 1580, 1584), so they cannot have compared crack itself. Route-specific physical harms (respiratory, cardiovascular, injection-related) are not reviewed; the review only notes that routes have specific medical manifestations (p. 1586).

interpretation_gap.results_show: The cited laboratory studies show similar pharmacology for smoked base and intravenous hydrochloride, faster and stronger effects for both than for intranasal use, and a preference for smoked doses in one choice study. The cited survey, treatment and administrative data show that people who smoke crack, or inject, use more often and in larger amounts, reach regular use and treatment sooner, and appear more often in emergency, psychiatric, infection and crime statistics, mostly in uncontrolled comparisons from selected samples of the mid-1980s to early 1990s.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says evidence exists, and the Comment opens "It is very clear that both smoked crack cocaine" and intravenous hydrochloride carry greater liability to repeated use, more substantial dependence and more severe consequences than intranasal use (pp. 1580, 1586), whereas the last Results paragraph says study limitations (no separation of intravenous from intranasal use, polydrug use, several routes in the same people, after-the-fact analysis) make it difficult "to come to any specific or clear-cut conclusions" (p. 1586). The abstract's conclusion that intranasal hydrochloride "may be a gateway drug or behavior" to crack rests on sequence data (most people who smoked crack had snorted first), which cannot show that one leads to the other. The Comment attributes similar HIV rates in people smoking crack and people injecting to sexual activity in causal terms from cross-sectional associations (p. 1586), and the source cited for similar HIV rates (ref 64) is, by its title, a gonorrhoea study (pp. 1585, 1588). The policy conclusions (a 2–3:1 ratio; treatment rather than prison) go beyond the reviewed evidence: the ratio comes from the share of past-month among ever use of crack and of other cocaine in the 1994 NHSDA (11.1% vs 4.5%), a method the authors call not optimal (p. 1586).

timeline.event: Foltin and Fischman, laboratory choice between smoked and intravenous cocaine in experienced participants (ref 25; second author's laboratory; not read)

Evans et al., J Pharmacol Exp Ther: arterial and venous cocaine concentrations by route; this review cites only the same first author's 1993 meeting abstract on arterial kinetics of smoked and intravenous cocaine (ref 24); being carded in this round

US household survey of people who had just started cocaine: a recent start of crack went with more dependence features than a start of powder only (adjusted odds ratio 1.6–1.9); its authors call this consistent with the present review
Systematic review with meta-analyses of health outcomes of crack use cites this review as background; it found comparisons of crack with other cocaine use mixed and did not pool them

replication.where_it_stands: Still the most cited summary of the crack-versus-powder question among the sources read for this round. Its central pharmacological point, that the two forms are one drug and that route, speed of delivery and amount explain most differences, is consistent with the laboratory studies it cites. Its statements about dependence and consequences rest on uncontrolled comparisons that later work addressed only in part: a population study of new starters found an excess of dependence features with crack that shrank after adjustment for days of use (Chen and Anthony, 2004), and a 2017 systematic review found comparisons of crack with other cocaine use mixed (Butler et al., 2017). Numbers should be taken from the primary studies.

funding.funder: Not reported. The acknowledgement thanks Paul R. Pentel (Hennepin County Medical Center) and Susan A. Dudish (University of Minnesota) for editorial assistance (p. 1587).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry, University of Minnesota (Hatsukami); Department of Psychiatry, Columbia University, and New York State Psychiatric Institute (Fischman) (p. 1580). Fischman co-authored at least five of the cited studies (refs 8, 17, 18, 20, 25), including the smoked-versus-intravenous choice study at the centre of the section on liability to repeated use, and an unpublished observation of hers (M.W.F.) is used to explain its result (p. 1583); Hatsukami co-authored ref 47. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts of people starting cocaine that record form, route, amount and frequency over time, measure pre-existing risk (other drug use, psychiatric history, social circumstances), and compare dependence and health outcomes by route with amount used treated as a possible mediator; and a systematic review with appraisal and pooling of the direct comparisons of smoked crack with snorted and injected hydrochloride that this review summarizes narratively.

domains.note: A MEDLINE search (1976–1996, four terms, author names), reference lists, manual searches and an annotated bibliography are named, with an inclusion criterion; but one database only, no counts, no list of included studies, a criterion that differs between abstract and Methods, many cited sources outside it, and almost all studies found said to be included.

No study is appraised and designs and sample sizes are mostly not given; general limitations are named (p. 1586) and one small half-life study and the age of the surveys are flagged, but uncontrolled comparisons from treatment, hotline, jail and street samples are summarized as findings and the main conclusion is called very clear.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The laboratory comparison of smoked and intravenous cocaine rests on the second author's studies and on an unpublished observation of hers; the epidemiological and consequence sections draw on other groups.

Policy recommendations are set apart (Implications for Policy) and the 2–3:1 ratio is said to rest on a non-optimal method, but untested explanations (for overdoses by route, for HIV rates through sexual activity) and the gateway interpretation are presented as conclusions.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence that crack itself differs against evidence that route, amount and context explain the differences (the former under-represented)
domains.note: Evidence of greater harm with crack is reported but attributed to route, amount or social context without any test; the support for no differences once amount is controlled is thin and partly predates crack; harms specific to smoking or injecting are not reviewed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The editors' checklist is used rather than AMSTAR 2 because, although a search is described, its yield and the included studies cannot be identified, the stated criterion does not govern the evidence cited, and the conclusions rest largely on sources outside the search (as for sc_peltoniemi_2016; unlike sc_murphy_2009, which reports counts and a table of every included study). The review states clearly the pharmacological argument that the two forms are one drug and that route, speed and amount matter, and points to useful primary studies; but nothing in it is appraised, its strongest conclusions go beyond the limitations it states, and its policy recommendations are opinion. Cite it for the argument and as a pointer to the laboratory and survey studies it names; take numbers from the primary studies; do not cite it for the size of any crack–powder difference, for a gateway effect or for route-specific medical harms. A claim resting only on this review stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3).

key_findings.finding: The authors describe a MEDLINE search for 1976–1996 with four search terms and selected authors' names, reference lists, manual searches and an annotated bibliography, with inclusion limited to studies comparing crack with intravenous or intranasal cocaine hydrochloride; they say so few studies existed that almost all were included and that most date from the mid to late 1980s and early 1990s. No counts or list of included studies are given.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Objective and Study Selection; Data Sources (four paragraphs); Data Extraction

key_findings.finding: In the 1993 NHSDA (civilian non-institutionalized population aged 12 and over), of people who had used cocaine in the past year 77% snorted, 36% smoked and 7% injected it; past-year crack use was 0.3% of white, 1.6% of Black and 0.6% of Hispanic people (an estimated 473,079, 368,032 and 111,006 people). The review cites an analysis finding that crack use did not differ by race or ethnicity once drug availability and social conditions were held constant (ref 6).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st paragraph (p. 1580, population definition); Results › Prevalence of Cocaine Use, 1st paragraph (p. 1581)
key_findings.note: The scan prints thousands with thin spaces (473 079, 368 032, 111 006); the machine-read text keeps the space in some and drops it in others, so a mechanical number search may miss them. Checked on the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: As the review describes US federal law: under the 1986 sentencing guideline a first offender possessing 5 g of crack received the same 5-year mandatory minimum as one possessing 500 g of cocaine hydrochloride (a 100:1 ratio), and a 1988 law set a 5-year minimum for possessing more than 5 g of crack against at most 1 year for simple possession of hydrochloride; the review reports 22 times more convictions of African Americans than of whites under the guideline, with Black defendants 88% of federal crack distribution convictions in 1993 (Hispanic 7%, white 4%) against 27% of hydrochloride charges (white 32%, Hispanic 39%).

The review states that cocaine hydrochloride cannot be smoked because it decomposes at vaporizing temperatures, whereas the base form can, so form dictates route; once absorbed the two forms have similar elimination and metabolic profiles: several studies found no difference in elimination half-life between smoked base and intravenous hydrochloride, one small study found 56 vs 78 minutes for smoked vs intranasal, and urinary excretion of cocaine and metabolites was 64%–69% of the dose for all three routes in one study.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 5th paragraph (p. 1581); Results › Cocaine Hydrochloride and Cocaine Base: Are They the Same Drug?, 1st–3rd paragraphs (pp. 1581–1582)
key_findings.note: Primary studies (refs 7–9) not read; the review itself flags the half-life study as small.

key_findings.finding: As summarized from cited studies: bioavailability of smoked base 60–70%, and of intranasal cocaine from 25% to 80–94% across studies, with a larger fraction of a higher intranasal dose absorbed in one study (58% of 96 mg vs 30% of 64 mg); peak venous concentration about 30–40 minutes after intranasal use and about 5 minutes after intravenous or smoked use; peak effects of intranasal cocaine at 15–40 minutes (physiological) and 10–20 minutes (subjective), lasting about 60 minutes or longer after the peak, against effects within minutes lasting about 30–45 minutes after intravenous or smoked use.
key_findings.locator: Is Crack More Addictive Than Cocaine Hydrochloride? › Pharmacokinetics, Pharmacodynamics, and Psychotropic Effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures from refs 7, 9, 14, 17–23 (not read); conditions, doses and assays differ across them.

key_findings.finding: One study, cited only as a 1993 meeting abstract (ref 24), found peak arterial concentrations about 10 times venous after both smoked and intravenous cocaine, reached within 15 seconds against 3–6 minutes for venous; its investigators concluded the two routes could not be told apart in liability to repeated use.
key_findings.locator: Pharmacokinetics, Pharmacodynamics, and Psychotropic Effects, 3rd paragraph (p. 1582); reference 24 (p. 1587)

key_findings.finding: In the only laboratory choice study cited (ref 25, the second author's laboratory), people experienced with both routes chose smoked doses as often as intravenous doses giving substantially higher plasma levels, and chose smoked over intravenous at doses giving similar plasma levels and effects (50 mg smoked vs 32 mg intravenous), although 80% said they preferred intravenous use outside the laboratory; the discrepancy is explained by an unpublished observation of the second author (M.W.F.).
key_findings.locator: Pharmacokinetics, Pharmacodynamics, and Psychotropic Effects, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Surveys summarized: three times as many New York State students in grades 7–12 who used cocaine had tried crack after other forms as the reverse (44% vs 13%; 7611 students); 75–90% of people who smoked crack had first used cocaine intranasally; in two VA samples 70–80% began intranasally and 60–70% were smoking at admission; in one of them 84% of those who began by smoking, 64% of those who began by injecting and 19% of those who began intranasally kept their first route, and 52% of intranasal starters switched to smoking; in London, people who first used cocaine after 1987 were more likely to have begun by smoking.
key_findings.locator: Pattern of Drug Use › Progression From Cocaine Hydrochloride to Crack, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Progression: regular use (3 or more times a week) was reached faster with crack than with intranasal or intravenous use in Miami street and treatment samples, and sooner with smoked use among jail inmates; smoked or intravenous use went with faster onset of problems and treatment entry; one study found no route difference in self-reported withdrawal and tolerance; the review concludes that how quickly dependence develops may depend more on rapid absorption than on the form of cocaine.
key_findings.locator: Pattern of Drug Use › Progression: Experimentation to Dependence, 2nd paragraph (p. 1583), 5th and 6th paragraphs (p. 1584)

key_findings.finding: Amount: people who smoke or inject cocaine typically use more than people who snort it (two thirds of people smoking crack used daily against 18% of people snorting powder; in the 1991 NHSDA crack use was 52.5% among frequent vs 17.5% among infrequent past-year cocaine use, injection 24.3% vs 9.3%), although one Miami sample reported the largest 90-day totals among people snorting; the review states that when amount used is controlled, no differences in consequences remain across routes.
key_findings.locator: Progression: Experimentation to Dependence, 4th paragraph (pp. 1583–1584); Characteristics and Consequences, 2nd paragraph (p. 1584)
key_findings.note: The 'no differences once amount is controlled' statement cites refs 39, 53 and 54; in the reference list (p. 1588) refs 53 and 54 are proceedings of the 1982 and 1983 meetings, before crack appeared by the review's own account (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: 1992 DAWN: of cocaine-related emergency-room mentions, 37% involved smoking, 18% injection and 11% snorting (other 4%, unknown 30%); among cocaine-related deaths injection was the most frequent route, but route was unknown for 73%; a Miami street and treatment sample (1988–1990) reported most self-reported overdoses with intravenous use, then intranasal, then crack.

In treatment-seeking samples, people preferring smoking had the highest rates of intermittent depressive personality disorder and the lowest of alcoholism and antisocial personality disorder; among people entering therapeutic communities, suicide attempts were 2 to 4 times as frequent with crack as primary drug as with other primary drugs; 88% of 40 people with cocaine dependence admitted to a psychiatric ward were using crack.

Sexual health and pregnancy: in a 1991 survey, people smoking crack reported more sex partners, more unprotected sex and more exchange of sex for drugs or money than people injecting cocaine who did not smoke it; neonatal hospital costs were $6735 vs $1226 and stays 7.9 vs 2.9 days when mothers reported crack rather than other cocaine, adjusted for prenatal care, maternal alcohol and cigarette use, race, gravidity, maternal age and infant sex; the review calls the effects of cocaine on neonates controversial.

Crime: the review attributes most crack-related violence to the drug market and to crime driven by the need for money, calling violence directly induced by cocaine's pharmacology uncommon; federal crack offenders more often carried weapons (27.9% vs 15.1%) and more often had the highest criminal-history category (17.6% vs 7.0%) than hydrochloride offenders; crack sellers had engaged in deviant behaviour before crack, which the review reads as recruitment of people already involved in crime.

The review states that most studies did not separate intravenous from intranasal hydrochloride use, and that polydrug use, use of several routes by the same people and after-the-fact analysis make careful interpretation difficult, so that specific or clear-cut conclusions are hard to reach.

Comment: smoked crack and intravenous hydrochloride are said to have, very clearly, greater liability to repeated use, greater propensity to produce substantial dependence and more severe social and personal consequences than intranasal hydrochloride; the differences are attributed to speed and intensity of delivery, unit price and accessibility, and social context rather than to the form of cocaine.
key_findings.locator: Comment › Differences Between Crack and Cocaine Hydrochloride, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors propose, as a possibility based on a method they call not optimal, a 2–3:1 rather than 100:1 crack-to-powder sentencing ratio, derived from the share of people who had ever used each form who had used it in the past month in the 1994 NHSDA (11.1% for crack vs 4.5% for other cocaine), and recommend treatment over imprisonment for people whose selling is driven by their own use.
key_findings.locator: Comment › Differences Between Crack and Cocaine Hydrochloride, 2nd paragraph (p. 1586); Implications for Policy, 2nd and 4th paragraphs (pp. 1586–1587)

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that people who smoke crack have rates of HIV infection as high as people who inject drugs cites ref 64, whose title describes risk factors for gonorrhoea among Black adolescents in San Francisco; the crack and HIV study in the list is ref 63 (Edlin et al., 1994).
reporting_issues.consequence: The HIV comparison cannot be traced to its cited source; a claim on HIV prevalence must rest on a primary HIV study read in full.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods restrict inclusion to studies comparing crack with intravenous or intranasal hydrochloride, the abstract states a broader criterion and an English-language restriction the Methods omit, and many cited sources fit neither criterion (sentencing and survey reports, DAWN, crime, cost, treatment and modelling studies, an unpublished observation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The evidence base cannot be reconstructed from the stated methods; the review is treated as narrative.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that no differences remain across routes once amount is controlled cites refs 39, 53 and 54; refs 53 and 54 are proceedings of the 1982 and 1983 meetings of the Committee on Problems of Drug Dependence (published 1983 and 1984), before crack emerged in the mid-1980s by the review's own account.
reporting_issues.consequence: For crack specifically, the 'amount, not form' statement rests on at most one 1987 hotline survey (ref 39) and should not be cited as tested.

reporting_issues.issue: The last Results paragraph says the limitations of the studies make specific or clear-cut conclusions difficult, while the Comment that follows opens by calling the greater liability, dependence and harm of smoked and intravenous use very clear.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should follow the stated limitations rather than the Comment's certainty.
